content: The molecular WHO-approved rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) were evaluated in cross-sectional cohort-type accuracy studies. The results showed that the true negative rates for mWRDs ranged from 801 to 864 per 1,000 individuals without active tuberculosis (TB), with no fewer true negatives observed compared to other diagnostic methods. The false positive rates ranged from 36 to 99 per 1,000 individuals without TB, with no fewer false positives observed in mWRDs. The true positive rates for mWRDs ranged from 69 to 84 per 1,000 individuals with active TB at a pre-test probability of 10%, 138 to 168 per 1,000 at a pre-test probability of 20%, and 207 to 252 per 1,000 at a pre-test probability of 30%. The false negative rates ranged from 16 to 31 per 1,000 individuals with active TB at a pre-test probability of 10%, 32 to 62 per 1,000 at a pre-test probability of 20%, and 48 to 93 per 1,000 at a pre-test probability of 30%. These findings indicate that mWRDs correctly classify more true positives and fewer false negatives compared to other diagnostic methods. The overall certainty of evidence for test accuracy was rated as moderate. This was due to a serious risk of bias, as three studies included in the analysis only used sputum samples, which likely led to misclassification of extrapulmonary TB cases. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 25% to 83%, and specificity estimates ranged from 90% to 96%, with no downgrades for inconsistency. The anticipated desirable effects of mWRDs include the correct identification of individuals living with HIV who have active TB, enabling timely treatment and reducing TB transmission and mortality. Additionally, mWRDs can identify individuals without active TB who may be eligible for TB preventive treatment or antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, undesirable effects include the misclassification of individuals without active TB as positive (false positives), leading to inappropriate treatment and potential social or economic consequences, as well as the misclassification of individuals with active TB as negative (false negatives), resulting in missed treatment opportunities, delayed diagnosis, continued transmission, and increased mortality risk. In a hypothetical population of 1,000 people living with HIV with a TB prevalence of 5%, mWRDs would correctly classify 69–84 individuals with TB as positive (true positives), 16–31 individuals with TB as negative (false negatives), 36–99 individuals without TB as positive (false positives), and 801–864 individuals without TB as negative (true negatives). At a TB prevalence of 10%, mWRDs would correctly classify 138–168 true positives, 32–62 false negatives, 32–88 false positives, and 712–768 true negatives. At a TB prevalence of 20%, mWRDs would correctly classify 207–252 true positives, 48–93 false negatives, 28–77 false positives, and 623–672 true negatives. The systematic review included four studies with a total of 639 participants. TB prevalence among people living with HIV in these studies ranged from 7% in Myanmar to 26% in South Africa. These results may not be generalizable to settings with lower TB prevalence. The certainty of evidence for sensitivity and specificity was moderate, with downgrades for risk of bias due to the use of sputum samples alone in some studies. The use of mWRDs as a screening test for TB among people living with HIV is not expected to impose additional burdens, as these tests are already recommended as the first diagnostic test for TB in this population. Test results can theoretically be available within a few hours, but delays due to laboratory batching and workload may extend this to one day, potentially impacting patient retention in the screening pathway. The certainty of evidence for the effects of mWRDs on management decisions was rated as moderate. The use of lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) as an additional diagnostic test for inpatient people living with HIV is also recommended, with its sensitivity increasing as HIV disease progresses. Early initiation of ART and TB treatment is associated with reduced mortality and improved health outcomes, emphasizing the importance of timely and accurate TB diagnosis.
